title: Show CPU model, cores and virtualization support on Linux
summary: Shows the processor model, the number of cores and threads, and whether the CPU supports hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V). Hardware virtualization makes virtual machines such as KVM or VirtualBox run faster.

aliases.text: how to check my cpu model linux
what processor do I have linux
какой у меня процессор в линуксе

steps.explain: Shows the processor details. Find 'Model name' (the CPU model), 'CPU(s)' (total threads), and 'Core(s) per socket'. Look at 'Virtualization': VT-x means Intel, AMD-V means AMD.
steps.expect: Lines like 'Model name: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-...' and 'Virtualization: VT-x' or 'Virtualization: AMD-V'. No Virtualization line means it is not supported or is disabled in BIOS/UEFI.

alternatives.explain: Checks the CPU flags without lscpu. vmx is Intel VT-x, svm is AMD-V. The number is how many logical CPUs report the flag; 0 means no hardware virtualization or it is disabled in BIOS/UEFI.
alternatives.expect: A number above 0 (one per logical CPU) on Intel or AMD processors with virtualization enabled. grep exits with status 1 when the count is 0.

alternatives.explain: Run inxi with the --cpu flag to print a summary of CPU information.

verify.expect: A 'Model name:' line with your CPU name. A 'Virtualization:' line appears only if VT-x or AMD-V is supported and enabled.

source.title: lscpu manual; card written and verified in the lnxhelp sandbox

warnings: On minimal Fedora systems lscpu may be missing; it is provided by the util-linux package.
